rows.description: You think the other side is stupid or evil. Contempt feels superior but blinds you to real grievances and persuades no one. Try to explain their strongest view before disagreeing; that keeps you honest and humane.

Being dismissed as brainwashed or anti-national stings and closes you. You can end a conversation calmly, state your view briefly, and refuse to be defined by a label. Dignity does not require winning the exchange.

I laugh at a child who fell, because everyone else does. I feel part of the group but a little uneasy. A wise adult asks "how would you feel?" Laughing at pain is a habit copied from others and can be unlearned.

The class laughs when I mispronounce a word. I feel small and hot. A wise adult says "everyone is learning". I can laugh gently or say "that is unkind". Laughter that hurts is not the same as laughing together.
You were turned down and feel small. Wise: let yourself grieve, stop chasing, and take distance without blaming them. Immature: repeated messages, sulking, or telling everyone they led you on.
Someone says they do not feel the same and it stings. Wise: give a gracious no, without lying about reasons or leaving hope. Harmful: leading them on because you enjoy being wanted.
I want to make up with a sibling after years of silence. I reach out with a short humble note, own my part, and do not demand a full accounting; trust returns through steady small acts.

A relative I fell out with offers a bridge and I feel wary. I can welcome the gesture and still move slowly, asking for honesty and change; I am free to decide the level of closeness I can safely offer.

I have cut contact with a parent after long pain and feel relief mixed with grief. The choice can be necessary for safety and peace; I check that I am acting from clarity and not from anger, and leave the door open only if it is safe.

My child or sibling has cut me off and I feel bewildered and hurt. I listen without defending, apologise for what I did, stop pressuring them via relatives, and let them come back at their pace if they choose.
You use guilt, sulking or threats to get what you want. Wise: ask directly, accept a no, and see the fear behind it. Harmful: winning by hurting.
They twist your words and you feel confused and guilty. Wise: notice patterns, keep notes, talk to trusted people outside, and trust your perception. It is not your fault.
